title: My thoughts on vertical non-permanent surfaces
author: Craig Barton
summary: After watching five lessons in a Swedish school, three of which had students working in groups at vertical whiteboards, Craig Barton gives a candid critique of Peter Liljedahl's vertical non-permanent surfaces. He lists the claimed benefits, then declares his bias against group work and the limits of a small sample. His concerns are the lack of individual accountability, easy copying from neighbouring groups, the long time taken (23 minutes plus 8 for feedback in one lesson) and doubt about the measures of effectiveness, since students liking an approach does not make it effective. He proposes either a few minutes of silent individual thinking before the boards or a 4-2 cycle of individual work then paired comparison on mini-whiteboards.
points: Barton's main objection is that group work at the boards lets weaker or lazier students hide while a quick student does the thinking.
Visible work is a double-edged sword, since neighbouring groups can copy answers; the same visibility that aids the teacher aids copying.
Opportunity cost matters: 31 minutes on ten circle questions could be halved, freeing time for harder problems or retrieval practice.
Student preference and unmeasured collaboration benefits are weak justifications compared with evidence on learning.
His alternative, the 4-2 approach, pairs silent individual work on mini-whiteboards with short structured paired discussion.
quotes: I have a bias against group work. Despite conversations with group-work advocates such as Sammy Kempner, I have never been able to make group-work effective in my lessons. This is probably my failing as a teacher.

However, when groups can get away with offloading all the work and thinking to one student, this does not happen. Perhaps you can tell from the photo at the top of this post that some students are working hard, and some students are having a chat.

A question I ask in all lessons I watch is: How easy would it be for a student to hide a lack of effort or a lack of understanding? In the VNPS phase of these three lessons, I think it would be very easy.
One of the stated advantages of VNPS is that student work is visible to the teacher. However, this means it is also visible to other groups.
I am obsessed with how time is spent in lessons. Every teacher's decision has an opportunity cost, as that time can not be spent doing something else.

Students like a lot of things, but that does not mean they are good for their learning. Students prefer to revise by rereading and highlighting, whereas we know practice testing and self-explanation are more effective strategies.

First, if you want to stick with the VNPS and overall structure of the lesson, then I think giving each student a copy of the worksheet at their desks and allowing them, say, 5 minutes of individual silent thinking time before asking them to form a group at the boards would help.
